questions.passage: In what is now southern Florida, the Calusa people (circa 1000-1600 CE) supported their relatively large population's dietary needs with hydrological engineering rather than terrestrial farming methods. They constructed watercourts (gated coastal enclosures) out of shells and sediments to trap a variety of fish as waters rose and fell with tides and seasonal sea-level shifts; watercourt pools then held the fish for later consumption. Archaeologist Theresa Schober has posited an additional purpose of these enclosures, suggesting that they were intended to foster conch. choices.label: C

choices.label: D

choice_analysis.A: Incorrect. A greater diversity of sea snails inside watercourts could support, rather than weaken, a cultivation hypothesis.
choice_analysis.B: Correct. It directly challenges whether the enclosures could sustain the habitat conch need.
choice_analysis.C: Incorrect. Mixed shell fragments and conch not being the majority do not rule out an intended conch-fostering purpose.
choice_analysis.D: Incorrect. Changes in open-water abundance after construction do not directly address whether watercourts were designed to foster conch.

explanation.short: B directly challenges whether the watercourts could support the habitat conch need.
explanation.detailed: To weaken Schober's hypothesis, the finding must show that watercourts were unlikely to foster conch. B does this by stating that their dimensions suit fish but not the shallow, seagrass-rich conditions sea snails require.

Trait | Day 5 | Day 10 | Day 15 | Day 20 Total number of open male and female flowers per growth unit | 25 | 65 | 110 | 45 Estimated reproductive success rate of male flowers | 0.29 | 0.29 | 0.29 | 0.29 Proportion of male flowers | 0.45 | 0.50 | 0.48 | 0.13

The mating environment hypothesis predicts that populations of flowering plants compensate for reduced mating opportunities due to dichogamy (a plant's expression of male and female functions at separate times to prevent self-pollination) by adjusting the bias of floral sex allocation during the flowering period, increasing the probability of successful cross-plant pollination. Researchers tested the hypothesis by examining a population of broadleaf arrowhead, a plant for which bloom onset generally takes longer for male flowers than for female flowers, during the flowering season. They concluded that the mating environment hypothesis is not well supported by their observational data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sex allocations were largely evenly distributed on days 10 and 15 but were female biased on days 5 and 20.

explanation.key_evidence: By day 20, the proportion of male flowers fell to 0.13, but the estimated reproductive success rate of male flowers stayed 0.29 on every measured day.
explanation.why_correct: Choice C supports the conclusion because it shows a major shift in sex allocation without any change in male reproductive success, undermining the hypothesis that allocation changes improve mating success.

choice_analysis.A: Incorrect. It identifies two peaks but does not connect the allocation shift to reproductive success.
choice_analysis.B: Incorrect. It notes no decline from day 15 to day 20, but it focuses on total flowers rather than the key sex-allocation pattern across the period.

explanation.short: C links the female-biased allocation by day 20 to unchanged male reproductive success.
explanation.detailed: The researchers concluded that the mating environment hypothesis was not well supported. The table shows that even when sex allocation became strongly female-biased by day 20, male reproductive success stayed constant at 0.29. That pattern supports C.

• - Brussels sprouts are vegetables that contain ascorbic acid, an essential nutrient for humans. - Grapes are fruits that contain ascorbic acid. - There is 80 milligrams (mg) of ascorbic acid per every 100 grams (g) of brussels sprouts. - There is 10 mg of ascorbic acid per every 100 g of grapes. - Humans cannot make ascorbic acid in their bodies, so they must get it from foods, including fruits and vegetables. - Ascorbic acid is also known as vitamin C.
questions.prompt: The student wants to refute a claim that grapes are a better source of vitamin C than brussels sprouts are. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Humans cannot make ascorbic acid in their bodies, but they can get it from brussels sprouts and grapes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brussels sprouts contain vitamin C (also known as ascorbic acid); in fact, there is 80 mg of vitamin C in every 100 g of brussels sprouts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Brussels sprouts contain ascorbic acid (also known as vitamin C), and grapes do too.

choices.label: D
choices.text: With 80 mg of vitamin C per every 100 g, brussels sprouts are actually a better source of vitamin C than grapes, which contain only 10 mg per every 100 g.

explanation.key_evidence: The notes say brussels sprouts have 80 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, while grapes have 10 mg per 100 g.
explanation.why_correct: Choice D directly refutes the claim by comparing both foods and showing that brussels sprouts contain more vitamin C.

choice_analysis.A: Incorrect. It says both foods contain vitamin C but does not compare amounts.
choice_analysis.B: Incorrect. It gives only the brussels sprouts amount, so it does not fully refute the claim about grapes.
choice_analysis.C: Incorrect. It merely says both contain vitamin C.
choice_analysis.D: Correct. It uses the comparative numerical evidence needed to refute the claim.

explanation.short: Choice D directly refutes the claim by comparing both foods and showing that brussels sprouts contain more vitamin C.
explanation.detailed: The notes say brussels sprouts have 80 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, while grapes have 10 mg per 100 g. Choice D directly refutes the claim by comparing both foods and showing that brussels sprouts contain more vitamin C.

questions.passage: Snow hydrologist Julie Koeberle helps maintain automated snow measurement stations. * They are called SNOTEL sites. * There are around 90 stations throughout Wyoming. * One is at Castle Creek. * The data collected can help researchers make downstream water supply predictions.
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses information from the given sentences to provide an example of a SNOTEL site?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: The data collected by SNOTEL sites can help researchers predict downstream water supplies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Located throughout Wyoming, SNOTEL sites monitor snow conditions.

explanation.key_evidence: The notes identify Castle Creek as one of the SNOTEL sites among about 90 automated snow measurement stations in Wyoming.
explanation.why_correct: Choice B provides a specific example of a SNOTEL site by naming Castle Creek.

choice_analysis.A: Incorrect. It defines SNOTEL sites generally but does not give a specific example.
choice_analysis.B: Correct. It names Castle Creek as a SNOTEL site and situates it among Wyoming stations.
choice_analysis.C: Incorrect. It describes what SNOTEL data can do, not an example of a site.
choice_analysis.D: Incorrect. It gives general location and function information but no specific site.

explanation.short: Choice B provides a specific example of a SNOTEL site by naming Castle Creek.
explanation.detailed: The notes identify Castle Creek as one of the SNOTEL sites among about 90 automated snow measurement stations in Wyoming. Choice B provides a specific example of a SNOTEL site by naming Castle Creek.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• - The nautical mile (6,076 feet) is the measure of distance used in seafaring navigation. - A nautical mile directly correlates to one minute (1/60th of a degree) of latitude. - The curvature of Earth affects the accurate measurement of long distances when using flat maps. - Measuring distances with latitude and longitude coordinates takes into account Earth’s curvature. - Mariners use nautical charts marked with latitude and longitude to quickly calculate distances and positions.
questions.prompt: The student wants to explain why nautical miles are used to measure distances in seafaring navigation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Using nautical miles for navigation at sea takes Earth’s curvature into account, whereas measuring distances with latitude and longitude coordinates does not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nautical charts use latitude and longitude to measure long distances; these charts are more accurate than flat maps for measuring distances in seafaring navigation because they account for Earth’s curvature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since they directly correlate to the coordinates on nautical charts, which take into account Earth’s curvature, nautical miles are an efficient way to calculate distances at sea.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nautical miles are a measure of distance equal to one minute of latitude, which is a feature nautical charts use to calculate distances and positions.

explanation.key_evidence: The notes say a nautical mile correlates to one minute of latitude and nautical charts use latitude and longitude to account for Earth's curvature.
explanation.why_correct: Choice C explains why nautical miles are useful: they directly align with coordinates on nautical charts used for seafaring navigation.

choice_analysis.A: Incorrect. It falsely suggests latitude and longitude do not account for Earth's curvature.
choice_analysis.B: Incorrect. It explains nautical charts but does not connect nautical miles to the coordinate system.
choice_analysis.C: Correct. It links nautical miles to nautical-chart coordinates and Earth's curvature, explaining their navigational use.
choice_analysis.D: Incorrect. It defines nautical miles but does not fully explain why that makes them useful in seafaring navigation.

explanation.short: Choice C explains why nautical miles are useful: they directly align with coordinates on nautical charts used for seafaring navigation.
explanation.detailed: The notes say a nautical mile correlates to one minute of latitude and nautical charts use latitude and longitude to account for Earth's curvature. Choice C explains why nautical miles are useful: they directly align with coordinates on nautical charts used for seafaring navigation.
